author: Sam Graham
title: Rehab process for pair of bobcat kittens expected to be costliest in Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center history - NewsBreak
text:
By Sam Graham ,
1 hours ago ROANOKE, Va. ( WFXR ) — The Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center says it’s estimating a year-long process and a price tag north of $20,000 to return a pair of bobcat kittens recently taken into its care back to the wild, making it one of the longest and most expensive rehab projects in the center’s history.
The Wildlife Center received the kittens after they were found on the side of the road in Russell County by their deceased mother, who had been hit by a car.
“We don’t know how long they had been with the mother, but they were in pretty rough shape,” said Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center education director Megan Johnston.
Photo Credit: Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center So far, the kittens have progressed well since arriving in Roanoke on June 6, gaining weight and moving closer to eating solid food, but the Wildlife Center team says they still have a long road ahead.
Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center preps for busy ‘baby season’ “They take a long time to reach full maturity and be on their own,” said Johnston. “And they also learn a lot of their behaviors from their parents in the wild. So, losing that parent to imprint on and to learn from is really devastating for them.”
In terms of cost, food is the primary driver. Once the kittens begin eating solid foods, they will each require the equivalent of a whole chicken per day, ultimately needing to consume food they would hunt in the wild, like quail and rabbits, in the final few months of their rehab process.
Photo Credit: Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center The high price tag also covers medicine, exams and staff hours to look after them. That includes the great lengths those employees and volunteers will take to avoid the bobcats ‘imprinting’ on humans.
“They learn a lot based off what’s taking care of them as they’re growing up,” said Johnston. “So, if they see humans feeding them, they learn that that’s where food comes from. And especially with animals like this, we don’t want them running up to humans once they get released.”
The Wildlife Center says it hopes to use this rehab process to remind the community of the resource they provide.
Photo Credit: Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center “We do usually get a bobcat a year where people don’t understand that we exist and maybe don’t realize that what they have is a wild cat versus a house cat,” said Johnston. “So just spreading the word, going and telling other people you know that there is a place they can bring wildlife really goes a long way.”
During the rehab, the Wildlife Center is asking the community for donations, both monetary and in-kind, but also says volunteerism goes a long way.
